runs.text: Iunto, ou apar da tranqueira, ou

lines.note: Sakugiwa is the area immediately beside a stockade. The Portuguese pairs junto with apar, both expressing proximity, and continues the description of the enclosure below.

runs.text: cerca de paos q̃ ſe faz ao derredor da fortaleza.

lines.note: The fence of stakes surrounds a fortress. The small q with its abbreviation mark is visible after paos; the draft retained only the detached mark.

runs.text: Obra, ou inuẽção, ou traça. Vt,

lines.note: Saku-i denotes workmanship, invention, or design. Enlargement supports a faint abbreviation mark over the e of inuẽção. Upright Rẽ- begins the Japanese renga example after italic Vt.
Renga, dangi nado no sakui ga yoi praises the construction of linked verse, preaching, and similar compositions. Acompo- begins the Portuguese rendering across the physical break.

runs.text: ſição ou traça dos verſos, pregaçaõ, &c. he boa.

lines.note: The composition or arrangement of the verses and sermon is good. The scan supplies the i in ſição; pregaçaõ retains the printed final-vowel tilde rather than modernizing its position.

runs.text: Couſa teſa, & facil de quebrar, como

lines.note: Sakui first describes something stiff or brittle and easy to break. The Portuguese reads facil, with final l rather than the draft's long s.
Wood exemplifies the brittle-material sense; sakui hito then introduces a lively or quick person, a distinct figurative application of the same adjective.
Expedito completes the personal description as ready, capable, or quick in action; it is a short continuation, not another entry.
Sakuji refers to building work. The concise Portuguese identifies construction rather than literary composition, distinguishing it from the surrounding saku vocabulary.
Sakujitsu is equated with kinoo, yesterday. The terminal Japanese spelling is retained without expanding it to a modern romanization.
This homophonous sakujitsu means the first day of the lunar month, explained by tsuitachi. The scan restores j in the headword and the missing letters in Tçuitachi.

runs.text: Aparelho que hum faz com ardil,

lines.note: Sakumai denotes an arrangement or preparation made with ingenuity. Ardil is read with the following inuenção rather than assumed to imply deception alone.
Sakumai ga yoi, alternatively warui, evaluates the preparation as good or bad. The paired Japanese adjectives govern the explanation on the following two rows.

runs.text: Ser a inuenção, ou traça do apercebimento,

lines.note: The Portuguese restates the invention or design involved in making preparations. Apercebimento belongs to this planning sense, not to a new Japanese headword.

runs.text: que hum faz, boa, ou ruim.

lines.note: This completes the judgment that someone's arrangements are good or poor, translating the yoi/warui alternatives above.
The verbal sakumai entry gives contracted principal forms and means preparing something ingeniously. The accented endings are retained rather than expanded in the transcription.

runs.text: ção, & engenho como bãquete, feſta, &c. pera

lines.note: The divided inuenção is completed, with a banquet or celebration as examples of an ingeniously arranged occasion. The abbreviated bãquete is not expanded.
The preparations are for many people. The uneven spacing is retained as muit agente from the supplied reading; it is understood as muita gente, not as a different Portuguese expression.
Sakumoo concerns the growing crop or harvest, explained through ke no ue. The supplied spaced Q eno is retained; noui- continues the agricultural Portuguese noun novidade below.
The crop consists of rice, wheat, grain, and similar produce. The scan reads arroz rather than arraz; Coto- begins this year's assessment in the next line.
Kotoshi wa sakumoo ga yoi says that this year's harvest is good. The Portuguese translation again divides novidade at the physical line ending.
This completes the statement of a good rice harvest. Novidade here is agricultural yield, not news or novelty in the modern everyday sense.
Sakumu is explained as kinoo no yume, yesterday's dream. The Portuguese follows the Japanese temporal expression directly.
The alternative gloss calls it a dream that has passed. The printed ß-shaped sort is retained rather than silently expanded or modernized.

runs.text: Obra, ou couſa feita com inuenção.

lines.note: Sakuna describes work made with invention or artifice. The definition introduces the adjective illustrated by a sermon, a poem, and a person below.
Sakuna dangi and sakuna uta mean an artfully composed sermon and poem. The translation's Prè- is divided here; its printed accent is retained.

runs.text: gação, ou verſo bem compoſto, ou de boa

lines.note: This completes pregação and describes a well-composed sermon or verse. Boa modifies composição on the next row, so the line remains part of the same explanation.
The gloss concludes with composition and artifice, then introduces sakuna hito. The Japanese expression applies the same resourcefulness to a person.

runs.text: Homem de boa traça, & inuenção. Item,

lines.note: The person has good powers of planning and invention. Item introduces an additional description rather than a separate Japanese lemma.
The additional description calls the person lively, capable, and resolute. These qualities complete sakuna hito and help distinguish it from the preceding material-work examples.
Sakunin is explained through tsukuru hito and glossed as a cultivator. The Portuguese fixes the agricultural sense despite the broader literal idea of a maker.
Saku no mono is a work or created thing. The honorific gosaku no mono begins a specifically Christian application and continues across the next physical row.

runs.text: Obra, ou creatura de Deos. Palaura q̃

lines.note: The divided Japanese mono is completed; the Portuguese identifies a work or creature of God. The abbreviated q̃ begins a usage statement continued below.
This says the preceding expression is current in the Church. It qualifies the Christian use of gosaku no mono rather than asserting that every use of saku is religious.

runs.text: Paos de tranqueira, ou cerca que

lines.note: Saku no ki means the wooden stakes of a stockade. Here saku denotes a defensive fence, unlike the work or creation senses immediately above.
The stakes form an enclosure around fortresses. The line completes the defensive-fence definition and is not connected with the following cherry-tree vocabulary.
Sakura is glossed as a cherry tree. The Portuguese historical spelling Cereijeira is retained without introducing a botanical species identification.

runs.text: Gorazes, ou pargos que tomão na

lines.note: Sakuradai names fish compared with sea breams. The following timing clause, not a modern taxonomic identification, specifies which fish the dictionary has in view.

runs.text: terceira lũa em Abril, ou Mayo.

lines.note: The fish are caught in the third lunar month, described here as April or May. The lunar wording and the source's seasonal correspondence are preserved.

runs.text: P. O andar vendo as cereijei-

lines.note: Sakuragari is going to view cherry trees in bloom. The locally italic P. is retained with the gloss; the supplied reference explains it as a poetic-usage marker.
Floridas completes the description of flowering cherry trees. The visible l after f corrects the draft's foridas; the broken cereijei-ras remains divided between physical rows.
Sakuragi can mean the cherry tree or its wood. The gloss explicitly includes both the living tree and its material.
Sakuran means disorder or disturbance, illustrated here by upheavals of war. It is unrelated in sense to the preceding sakura compounds.
Sakurei is precedent or attestation from an earlier work. The scan supports teſtimunho with h, not the draft's b, while the following lines specify the type of work.

runs.text: feita por algum antiguo como compoſição de

lines.note: The attested work was made by an earlier author, for example a poetic composition. The printed antiguo is retained rather than modernized to antigo.
Renga is the Japanese verse form named within the Portuguese explanation, so it is eligible for whole-word typeface review. The final abbreviation is retained as printed.

runs.text: Dar cõ a mão pera diante como

lines.note: Sakuri, sakuru, sakutta describes a forward scooping motion with the hand. The printed v is preserved as a principal-form abbreviation; the explanation continues at the top of column 2.
The definition from column 1 continues with the motion of throwing earth or water. Mizu wo begins a Japanese example of scooping or sprinkling water by hand.

runs.text: Botar agoa com a mão com-

lines.note: Sakuri kakuru completes the water-scooping example. The scan has initial long s, not capital I; the Portuguese ends in printed com-, whose expected comparative wording is not silently supplied.
The example concerns sprinkling water in a house; a woodworking sense follows. Enlargement confirms the anomalous printed Ao before brir below; intended Abrir is not silently substituted.

runs.text: brir pao, ou madeira com algum ferro dando

lines.note: This describes opening or gouging wood with an iron tool. Com algum is visible in the scan: the draft misread com and omitted the entire word algum.
The tool is thrust or worked forward. This completes the woodworking sense of sakuru, distinct from the preceding action of scooping water with the hand.
Sakurigana is a particular woodworking plane. The Portuguese cepilho identifies the implement without specifying a modern tool subtype beyond the source.
Sakuryoo is a carpenter's wage. Iornal means pay for work here; the initial is I rather than the draft's F, and the example continues below.
Sakuryoo wo dasu means paying carpenters. The final form is daſu, supported by the surviving u and the payment gloss, rather than the draft's daſi.
Sakurito describes acting alertly, briskly, and readily. The scan supports Eſperta rather than Eſperia; the final adverb is divided across the next line.
This completes expeditamente and introduces sakurito shita hito, a brisk and capable person. The Portuguese noun Homem is completed by its adjectives below.
The man is lively and capable. This short row completes the example rather than beginning the next adverbial entry.
Sakusakuto is given the same brisk, ready manner of action. The example repeats the adverb, divided after Sacuſa- at the physical margin.
Sakusakuto mono wo yuu hito ja describes a person who speaks readily and decisively. The Portuguese relative clause begins here and continues on the following row.
The translation specifies speaking promptly and resolutely. It confirms the adverb's force in the preceding Japanese sentence rather than a description of the content spoken.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Modo de ſe partir, ou cortar com

lines.note: A second sense introduces the manner of breaking or cutting something with the teeth. The instrument is completed on the next line.

runs.text: os dentes algũa couſa teſa, & madura como

lines.note: The object bitten is firm and ripe. This is the crisp-biting sense of sakusakuto, illustrated by fruit on the next physical row.
Pears and the fruit called Japanese figs illustrate the crisp texture. The historical descriptive name is preserved without forcing a modern species label into the transcription.
Sakusha is explained as tsukuru mono, a maker, and glossed as an artisan or a person who creates a work. Homẽ retains its abbreviation mark.

runs.text: que faz algũa obra. ¶ Item, Poeta que faz

lines.note: After the general maker sense, the entry introduces a poet skilled in composing a particular kind of verse. The verse names follow below.
Renga and the divided rengu name the verses within the Portuguese explanation. The scan shows chamão with final o, omitted by the draft; the Japanese names are upright.

runs.text: Item, Homem que tem boa traça, ou

lines.note: Gu completes rengu. The next sense is someone with good powers of design or invention, with its last noun continued on the following row.
The general inventive-person gloss ends; gosakusha then introduces the honorific Christian term for the Creator. Cria- is physically divided from dor below.

runs.text: dor: palaura que corre na Igreja.

lines.note: This completes Criador and says that the term is used in the Church. The usage statement pertains to gosakusha, not every sense of sakusha.

runs.text: Obra que hum faz como verſos, &c.

lines.note: Sakusei denotes a work one makes, such as verses. The initial of verſos is visibly v, correcting the draft's perſos.
Sakuseki is yesterday evening, explained as kinoo no yuube. The Portuguese tarde is read in conjunction with that explicit Japanese evening expression.

runs.text: Fruito, ou rendimento que fica ao

lines.note: The second sakuseki entry concerns agricultural proceeds retained by the cultivator. Its meaning is distinct from the homophonous expression for yesterday evening.

runs.text: laurador depois de pagar ao ſenhor o rendi-

lines.note: The retained produce is what remains after the cultivator pays the lord. The divided rendimento continues on the next row.
This completes the annual payment to the lord. The whole three-line definition concerns the cultivator's remaining yield after that obligation.
Sakuya means last night. The concise gloss distinguishes it from the previous entry's earlier-evening expression without adding a modern temporal rule.
Sadakana is explained by akirakana, clear or distinct. The scan reads clara, not the draft's elara, and the paired adjective follows below.
Distincta completes the clarity definition. The supplied st spelling is retained; the joined type is not normalized through a general long-s rule.
Sadakani is the adverb, equated with akirakani. The supplied italic apparatus Aduer. i is retained; the Japanese synonym is upright, and Clara- continues below.
Claramente is completed before the example sadakani miezu, not appearing or being seen clearly. The negative Portuguese example continues below.
The translation says not to appear clearly and distinctly. The marked e in diſtintamẽte abbreviates the final nasal material and is retained unexpanded.
Sadamari gives the intransitive principal forms for becoming settled or determined. The reflexive Portuguese distinguishes it from the following transitive verb.
Sadame gives the historical transitive forms for determining or settling something. The object of the Portuguese verbs is supplied on the next physical row.
Algũa couſa is the object of determining or settling. This short continuation completes the verb entry before the separate noun sadame.
The noun sadame means a determination or decision. It is a separate entry even though its spelling matches the preceding verb's stem.
Sadamete is initially glossed as certainly or without doubt. The following qualification is essential to understanding the dictionary's account of ordinary usage.

runs.text: poſto que o ſentido commum, & corrente he,

lines.note: The concessive phrase says that the common, current sense differs from the preceding certainty gloss. It leads directly to the weaker interpretation below.
The ordinary sense is perhaps or probably. The apparent tension with sem duuida is explicitly in the source and must not be harmonized away.

runs.text: Hum dos cinco liuros que enſinão a-

lines.note: Saden names a book the dictionary places among five books teaching government. The visible a- is retained at the line end without attempting to correct that historical classification.
Gouernar completes the statement about teaching how to govern. It is a short continuation of the book description, not a new headword.

runs.text: Sadǒ. i, Chajo. l, Chano yujo.

lines.note: Sadoo is explained by chajo and cha no yujo, a place for tea. The alternative marker is lowercase l, not capital I; the Portuguese locates this place below.
The place is for chanoyu in a Buddhist temple. Both Chanoyu and Tera occur within the Portuguese explanation; the scan shows italic Chanoyu but upright Tera, eligible for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Vaſo em que metem o Cha moido.

lines.note: Sahyoo is a container for powdered tea. Cha is a Japanese term within the Portuguese explanation, and the scan's typeface is retained rather than changed from language alone.
Sahoo is equated with katagi and yoodai and glossed as custom or manner. The scan restores the circumflex in Safô; the definition continues on f430, whose initial &c. is anticipated by the catchword.
